# Converting to FASTQ with fasterq-dump {#sec-fasterq-dump}

`fasterq-dump` reads an `.sra` file (or streams the run from NCBI) and writes
FASTQ. It replaced the older, single-threaded `fastq-dump`. It is **much**
faster, but it behaves differently, and a few of those differences catch people out.

## The basic command

```bash
fasterq-dump sra/SRR1039508 --threads 6 --temp tmp --outdir fastq --progress
```

| Option | Short | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--threads <n>` | `-e` | 6 | CPU threads. Match it to the CPUs you asked SLURM for |
| `--temp <dir>` | `-t` | current folder | Where to put **temporary files** (a lot of them; see below) |
| `--outdir <dir>` | `-O` | current folder | Where to write the FASTQ |
| `--progress` | `-p` | off | Progress bar (leave off in batch jobs: it fills the log) |
| `--force` | `-f` | off | Overwrite existing output |
| `--split-3` | `-3` | **on (the default)** | See below |
| `--split-files` | `-S` | | Every read of a spot to its own file, including unpaired |
| `--split-spot` | `-s` | | Both reads of a pair as consecutive records in **one** file |
| `--concatenate-reads` | | | Join read 1 and read 2 into one long read |
| `--include-technical` | | off | Also write technical reads (barcodes, UMIs; needed for some single-cell data) |
| `--size-check on\|off\|only` | | on | Check there's enough disk space before starting |
| `--disk-limit`, `--disk-limit-tmp` | | | Stop if output/temp would exceed a size (useful when quotas hide the real free space) |

You can give it either the **folder from `prefetch`** (`sra/SRR1039508`) or a
bare accession (`SRR1039508`). With a bare accession, if there's no local copy, it
streams from NCBI: fine for small runs, slower and more fragile for large ones.

## What files you get: split-3

For each **spot** (one cluster on the flow cell), the default `--split-3`
mode does:

| Spot has... | Goes to |
|---|---|
| Two reads (read 1 + read 2) | `SRR1039508_1.fastq` and `SRR1039508_2.fastq`, in matching order |
| Only one read (the other was removed by the submitter's filtering) | `SRR1039508.fastq` |

So **paired-end** data normally gives `_1` and `_2`, sometimes plus a small
`SRR...fastq` of orphan reads. **Single-end** data gives one `SRR....fastq`.
For a paired-end pipeline use `_1` and `_2` and set the orphans aside. Check
first that the orphan file is small; if it's most of the data, the run may not
really be paired (see [Special cases](special-cases.qmd)).

::: {.callout-important}
## The output is not compressed

There's no `--gzip` option in `fasterq-dump`. Compress afterwards:

```bash
pigz -p 6 fastq/SRR1039508*.fastq      # parallel gzip; or plain `gzip`
```

Until you do, the files are 3–5× bigger than they need to be.
:::

## Disk space {#disk-space}

This is where most failures come from. `fasterq-dump` writes large
temporary files and then the (uncompressed) FASTQ. NCBI's own guidance:

- the **final FASTQ** is roughly **7×** the size of the `.sra`,
- **temporary space** is roughly **1.5×** the final FASTQ again,
- so in total, plan for **~10–20× the `.sra` size** free while it runs.

For a 2.5 GB airway run that's tens of GB. Point `--temp` at a filesystem with
room: a local folder or external drive on a laptop; the **scratch** space
on a cluster (not `/tmp` on a compute node, which is often small). Temp files are deleted at the end. If a job is killed they may be
left behind as `fasterq.tmp.*`; delete them.

```bash
df -h .                  # free space here
du -sh sra/SRR1039508    # size of the .sra
```

## Read names

By default reads are named `@<accession>.<spot number> <spot number> length=<n>`:

```
@SRR1039508.1 1 length=63
CATTGCTGATACCACAGATGAATCCCTTCTAGAAAACAGAGTACTGGATGCAGCCCTTCACAG
+SRR1039508.1 1 length=63
HJJJJJJJJJJJJJJJJJJJJIJJJJJJJJJJJJJJJJJIJJJJJJJJJJIJJJJJJJJJJJJ
```

(Example read.) The original Illumina names are usually **not** kept. That doesn't
matter for pipelines. If a tool insists on a particular format,
`--seq-defline` and `--qual-defline` set a custom name (for example
`--seq-defline '@$ac.$si/$ri'` adds `/1` or `/2`).

## fasterq-dump vs the old fastq-dump

You'll see `fastq-dump` in older tutorials:

```bash
fastq-dump --split-3 --gzip SRR1039508          # old: one thread, slow, but can gzip
fasterq-dump SRR1039508                          # new: same split by default, many threads, no gzip
```

| | fastq-dump | fasterq-dump |
|---|---|---|
| Speed | slow (one thread) | fast (multi-threaded) |
| Default split | none (one file!) | `--split-3` |
| Gzip output | `--gzip` | no; compress afterwards |
| Subset of reads (`-X`, `-N`) | yes | no |
| Temp space | little | a lot |

`fastq-dump -X 1000 --split-3 SRR...` is still handy to grab the **first 1,000
spots** for a quick look without downloading everything.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Check your understanding

1. You run `fasterq-dump` on a paired-end run and get three files. What's the
   third, and should you use it?
2. A 10 GB `.sra` fails with "disk-limit exceeded". Roughly how much free space
   do you need?
3. Why ask SLURM for `-c 6` when running `fasterq-dump --threads 6`?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## Answers

1. `SRR....fastq`: reads whose mate is missing. For a paired-end pipeline, use
   only `_1` and `_2`; keep the third only if it holds a large fraction of reads
   (then investigate).
2. Something like 100–200 GB between output and temp, then far less once
   compressed.
3. So the six threads have six CPUs to run on; otherwise they compete for
   one, and it's no faster.
:::
:::
